- Why estimate theta on pooled data rather than per arm?
- What other covariates could you use besides the pre-period metric?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="eval-022" data-area="eval" data-skill="ab-testing" data-also="causal ads" data-type="tradeoff" data-level="staff" data-tracks="mle"}

::: {.rv-q}
When does a user-randomised A/B test give the wrong answer because of interference, and how do you design around it?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
A/B analysis assumes one unit's outcome does not depend on other units' assignments. It
fails when units share something.

**Where it fails.**

- *Two-sided marketplaces.* Treated riders who book more take drivers from control riders.
  Treatment looks better and control looks worse, so the measured effect overstates what a
  full launch would deliver.
- *Social and communication products.* A feature that makes treated users message more
  also raises activity among their control friends. The contrast shrinks and the effect is
  understated.
- *Shared budgets and inventory.* Ad budgets, stock, ranking slots.
- *Shared models and caches.* Both arms feed one training set or one cache, so the control
  arm is contaminated by the treatment's data.

**Designs.**

- *Cluster randomisation.* Randomise connected groups together: geographies, or clusters
  from the interaction graph. The cost is far fewer independent units, so lower power, and
  leakage across cluster boundaries remains.
- *Switchback.* Randomise time slices within a region, alternating treatment and control.
  Standard for marketplace pricing and dispatch. It needs a slice length longer than the
  carry-over and a washout or carry-over model.
- *Two-sided randomisation.* Randomise both sides (buyers and sellers) to estimate
  spillover.
- *Budget-split.* Give each arm its own share of budget or inventory so they do not
  compete.
- *Separate model or data pipelines* per arm when the feedback loop is the concern.

**Analysis.** Standard errors at the level of randomisation (cluster or time slice).

**Detecting interference.** Run the same change user-randomised and cluster-randomised;
a difference in estimates is evidence of spillover. Checking whether control-arm metrics
move as the treatment share ramps is another sign.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- How long should a switchback period be?
- A ranking model trains on data from both arms. What bias does that create?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="eval-023" data-area="eval" data-skill="ab-testing" data-also="ranking search-ir" data-type="tradeoff" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle"}

::: {.rv-q}
What is interleaving, why is it more sensitive than an A/B test for ranking, and what can it not tell you?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
Interleaving shows each user one result list merged from two rankers and infers preference
from which ranker's results get clicked.

**Team-draft interleaving.** For each query, the two rankers take turns, in an order
randomised per round, adding their highest-ranked result not yet in the list; each result
is tagged with the team that contributed it. Clicks are credited to teams. A query is a
win for the ranker with more credited clicks, and wins are compared across queries with a
sign or binomial test.

**Why it is more sensitive.** Each user is their own control. Differences between users
(heavy versus light clickers) and between queries, which dominate the variance of an A/B
test, cancel. Published reports from search and streaming companies describe needing one
to two orders of magnitude fewer samples than an A/B test for the same ranking comparison;
the factor depends on the product.

**What it cannot do.**

- It gives a relative preference, not the size of the effect on revenue, retention or
  sessions.
- It applies only to changes expressible as a reordering in the same slot. It cannot test
  latency, layout, or a new result type.
- It relies on clicks, with their position and attractiveness biases; it says nothing
  about satisfaction after the click.
- The merged list is not what either ranker would have shown, so whole-page effects such
  as diversity are distorted.
- It adds serving complexity.

**Use.** A fast filter: interleave many ranker candidates, discard the losers within days,
then run a conventional A/B test on the few winners to measure business metrics and
guardrails.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Why randomise which ranker picks first?
- Two rankers return nearly identical lists. What happens to the test?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="eval-024" data-area="eval" data-skill="ab-testing" data-also="statistics causal" data-type="debug" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle ai"}

::: {.rv-q}
An A/B test showed a significant win. Three months after launch the metric is back where it started. What happened, and how would you have caught it?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
**Candidate explanations.**

1. *Novelty.* Users engaged with something new and the effect decayed. Visible in the
   experiment as an effect that shrinks with days since first exposure.
2. *False positive.* Peeking, many metrics or segments examined, or many experiments run
   with the winners launched.
3. *Winner's curse.* Even a real effect is overestimated when it is selected for being
   significant, most strongly in underpowered tests. The true lift was smaller than
   reported.
4. *Launch differs from test.* At 100% the interference pattern changes (marketplace
   competition, shared budgets), capacity or latency is worse, or the launched code is
   not the tested code.
5. *Interaction.* Other launches since then removed or absorbed the gain.
6. *Population.* The test ran on a subset (new users, one platform, a triggered group)
   that does not represent everyone.
7. *Timing.* The test covered a holiday or campaign period.
8. *The metric moved for other reasons.* The trend is not a counterfactual: the launch
   may still be helping against a decline elsewhere, or the logging changed.

**Investigation.** Re-examine the original test: power, interval, pre-registration, the
effect by day and by cohort, sample ratio. Then measure the current effect directly with a
holdback or by turning the feature off for a small group.

**Catching it earlier.**

- A long-term holdback of 1-5% of users kept on control after launch.
- Running tests long enough to see the time trend, and analysing by exposure cohort.
- Replicating surprising wins before relying on them.
- Discounting reported lifts when forecasting cumulative impact; the sum of experiment
  wins always exceeds the realised gain.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- How do you distinguish novelty from a real effect inside a two-week test?
- Your team launched ten wins this quarter. How do you estimate the true total impact?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="eval-025" data-area="eval" data-skill="ab-testing" data-also="causal statistics" data-type="tradeoff" data-level="staff" data-tracks="mle ai"}

::: {.rv-q}
You cannot run an A/B test for this change. What are your options for estimating its effect?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
First ask why not, because the reason picks the method.

**No unit can be randomised fairly** (pricing, legal or ethical limits, a marketing
campaign).

- *Geo experiments*: randomise regions, or treat some regions and build a synthetic
  control from a weighted mix of untreated ones.
- *Staggered rollout*: release in a random order over time and compare not-yet-treated
  with treated.
- *Encouragement design*: randomise a nudge and use it as an instrument for uptake.

**The change already happened or was global.**

- *Difference-in-differences* against an unaffected group; requires parallel trends, which
  you check on the pre-period.
- *Interrupted time series* or Bayesian structural time series with control series;
  fragile to anything else that changed at the same time.
- *Regression discontinuity* when treatment was assigned by a threshold; estimates the
  effect near the threshold only.
- *Matching or inverse propensity weighting* on observational data; assumes no unobserved
  confounders, the weakest assumption of the set.

**Too little traffic.** Use more sensitive designs and metrics: within-subject comparison,
interleaving for ranking, variance reduction, a proxy metric closer to the change, a
longer test, or accept a larger minimum detectable effect and say so.

**A ranking or policy change with logged data.** Off-policy evaluation with inverse
propensity scoring or doubly robust estimators, which requires that the logging policy
was randomised with recorded propensities.

**An LLM product before launch.** Offline evals on replayed traffic, blinded human
side-by-side comparison, shadow mode, and a staged rollout with monitoring.

**For any of these.** State the identifying assumption, test it where possible (placebo
periods, placebo outcomes, pre-trend checks), report sensitivity, and present the result
with less confidence than a randomised test would earn.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- How do you test the parallel-trends assumption?
- What must be logged today to make off-policy evaluation possible later?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="eval-026" data-area="eval" data-skill="experimentation" data-also="research-eng training-dynamics" data-type="concept" data-level="core" data-tracks="mle ai re"}

::: {.rv-q}
How do you design an ablation study so that its conclusions can be trusted?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
An ablation attributes a result to a cause. It is trustworthy when the only difference
between two runs is the thing being claimed.

- **A strong, equally tuned baseline.** Most false gains come from a tuned new method
  against an untuned baseline. Give both the same tuning budget.
- **One change at a time.** If the new run changes the architecture, the learning rate and
  the data, the gain cannot be assigned. Either add components one by one to the baseline
  or remove them one by one from the full system; do both when interactions are likely.
- **Hold everything else fixed.** Data and splits, preprocessing, compute or step budget,
  evaluation code, decoding settings. Compare at equal parameters or equal compute, and
  say which.
- **Know the noise floor.** Run the baseline with several seeds (three to five at least)
  and measure the standard deviation of the metric. A difference smaller than about two
  standard errors is not evidence. For LLM applications the analogues are sampling
  variance and eval-set size.
- **Report all runs.** Mean and spread across seeds, not the best seed; include the
  variants that did not help.
- **Check the mechanism.** If the claim is "the gain comes from X", a control that removes
  X's supposed mechanism while keeping its parameter count or compute should lose the gain.
- **Record enough to reproduce.** Code commit, config, seeds, data version, environment.

Typical traps: test-set selection of checkpoints or hyperparameters, different amounts of
training between arms, an evaluation bug that favours one output format, and concluding
from a single seed.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Compute allows three seeds for one configuration or one seed for three. Which do you choose?
- Two components each give nothing alone and a gain together. How do you present that?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="eval-027" data-area="eval" data-skill="experimentation" data-also="statistics research-taste" data-type="tradeoff" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle ai re"}

::: {.rv-q}
You tried 30 variants and one beats the baseline by 0.4 points with p = 0.03. Do you believe it?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
Not yet. With 30 comparisons at $\alpha = 0.05$ and no real effects, the chance that at
least one looks significant is $1 - 0.95^{30} \approx 79\%$. A p-value of 0.03 for the
best of 30 is what noise produces.

**Corrections.**

- *Bonferroni*: require $p < \alpha/m = 0.0017$. Simple and conservative.
- *Holm*: step-down version, uniformly more powerful than Bonferroni.
- *Benjamini-Hochberg*: controls the false discovery rate, appropriate when screening many
  candidates and some false leads are acceptable.

**The better remedy is replication.** Select on one set of data and confirm on another:
rerun the winning variant and the baseline with new seeds, or evaluate on a held-out set
that played no part in choosing it. Expect the confirmed gain to be smaller than 0.4
because the best of many is biased upward.

**Also ask.**

- Is 0.4 above the noise floor from seed-to-seed variation of the baseline?
- Was the baseline tuned as much as the variants?
- Were the 30 variants chosen in advance, or did choices adapt to earlier results
  (stopping rules, metric choice, subsets)? Undisclosed flexibility inflates false
  positives beyond the simple count.
- Is there a reason to expect this variant to work? A mechanism raises the prior; an
  arbitrary winner lowers it.

**Pre-registration in an engineering setting.** Before the runs, write down the primary
metric, the eval set, the comparison, the decision threshold and the stopping rule.
Exploratory findings are fine, labelled as such and confirmed before anyone depends on
them.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- When is false discovery rate control the right choice over family-wise error control?
- How many seeds would you run to confirm a 0.4-point gain?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="eval-028" data-area="eval" data-skill="experimentation" data-also="research-eng exp-tracking" data-type="concept" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle re"}

::: {.rv-q}
A result from six months ago cannot be reproduced. What should have been recorded, and how do you make experiments reproducible by default?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
**What determines a result.** Code, configuration, data, randomness, environment and the
evaluation procedure. Each needs an identifier stored with the result.

- *Code*: the commit hash, plus a diff if the tree was dirty.
- *Configuration*: the fully resolved config after defaults and overrides, not only the
  command line.
- *Data*: dataset version or content hash, split definition, preprocessing and tokenizer
  versions, and any filtering.
- *Randomness*: seeds for initialisation, data order, augmentation and sampling.
- *Environment*: container image or lockfile, library versions, hardware type, precision
  settings.
- *Evaluation*: eval set version, metric code version, decoding settings, grader or judge
  version, checkpoint-selection rule.
- *For LLM applications*: model snapshot id, prompt and tool-definition versions,
  sampling settings, and stored raw outputs.

**Make it the default.** The launcher records all of this automatically to the experiment
tracker; runs from uncommitted code are refused or flagged; results tables are generated
from tracked runs and never typed by hand; each headline number links to its run.

**What reproducibility means.** Bit-exact reruns are often unattainable on GPUs
(non-deterministic kernels, different hardware, parallel data loading). The practical
target is statistical: a rerun lands within the seed-to-seed spread. That spread must be
known, which is another reason to run several seeds.

**When a result does not reproduce.** Diff the recorded items first; common culprits are
a changed dataset behind an unchanged name, a library upgrade, a default that changed, a
single lucky seed, and evaluation on a different checkpoint.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Which sources of non-determinism remain after fixing all seeds?
- How do you handle a dataset that is updated in place?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="eval-029" data-area="eval" data-skill="error-analysis" data-also="llm-evals data-analysis" data-type="concept" data-level="core" data-tracks="mle ai re"}

::: {.rv-q}
How do you do error analysis on a model or LLM system? Describe the procedure.
:::

::: {.rv-a}
Error analysis is reading failures systematically until you can say what the failure modes
are, how often each occurs and what each costs.

1. **Sample.** Take 50-100 failures (and some successes for contrast) from the eval set or
   production, sampled randomly within the failing set so the picture is not anecdotal.
2. **Read the raw material.** The full input, context, intermediate steps and output, not
   only the score. For agents, find the first step that went wrong; later errors are often
   consequences.
3. **Open coding.** Write a short free-text note per example on what went wrong. Do not
   start from a fixed list of categories.
4. **Build the taxonomy.** Group the notes into failure modes with clear definitions
   (retrieval miss, ignored instruction, wrong tool, format error, ambiguous request).
   Keep going until new examples stop producing new categories.
5. **Count and weigh.** Frequency times severity per mode gives the priority order.
6. **Slice.** Check whether a mode concentrates in an input type, language, length bucket,
   customer or tool.
7. **Act per mode.** Each mode gets a fix at the right layer (data, retrieval, prompt,
   tool, model) and test cases in the regression set, plus a targeted grader if it should
   be tracked.
8. **Repeat** after the fix; the distribution changes.

Useful habits: label for root cause, not symptom; check whether the label or the grader is
wrong (a fraction of "errors" are evaluation bugs); have a second person code a subset to
check the taxonomy is usable.

The usual mistake is skipping to dashboards and generic scores without reading examples,
or fixing the three most memorable failures instead of the most frequent.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- How many examples do you read before you trust the taxonomy?
- How would you use an LLM to scale this without losing accuracy?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="eval-030" data-area="eval" data-skill="error-analysis" data-also="labeling metrics" data-type="debug" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle ai re"}

::: {.rv-q}
The aggregate metric improved by a point after a model update, but complaints went up. How do you find out what happened, and how do you turn it into better data?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
An average can rise while an important group gets worse.

**Find the regression.**

- *Flip analysis.* Compare per-example results between versions. A net +1 point can be
  +6 points of fixes and -5 of new failures. Read the right-to-wrong set first.
- *Slice.* Per-slice deltas with confidence intervals across segment, language, input
  length, intent, customer tier, platform. Look for a small, valuable slice with a large
  drop.
- *Mix shift.* If slice proportions differ between the two measurements, the aggregate can
  move even when every slice is flat or worse (Simpson's paradox). Compare at fixed mix.
- *Automated discovery.* Cluster embeddings of the failures, or fit a shallow tree
  predicting error from metadata, to surface slices nobody predefined.
- *Coverage.* Check whether the complaining users' inputs are represented in the eval set
  at all. If not, the metric could not have seen the problem.
- *Severity.* The metric may count all errors equally while the new errors are worse.

**The long tail.** Head inputs dominate the average; rare inputs are individually
negligible and collectively large. Evaluate them deliberately: stratified sampling that
over-represents the tail, with weights to recover traffic-level numbers.

**Turn it into data.**

1. Add the failing cases to the regression set as a named slice with its own gate.
2. Mine production for more of the same (nearest neighbours of the failures, rule-based
   filters), label them, and split into training and evaluation with no overlap,
   including near-duplicates.
3. Use targeted synthetic variations and hard negatives for training only when real
   examples are scarce, and keep the eval real.
4. Track the slice on every release so the regression cannot return silently.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- How do you choose slices without testing hundreds and finding noise?
- What is the risk of adding mined failures to both training and evaluation?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="eval-031" data-area="eval" data-skill="human-eval" data-also="labeling llm-evals" data-type="design" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle ai re"}

::: {.rv-q}
Design a human evaluation programme for a generative model. How do you get labels you can trust?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
**Guidelines.** Define the task, each criterion and each scale level in observable terms,
with worked examples and explicit rulings for edge cases. Tell raters what to ignore.
Revise through pilot rounds: have several raters label the same 30-50 items, examine the
disagreements, and fix the wording that caused them.

**Raters.** Choose experts or trained generalists according to the knowledge needed. Use a
qualification test, and train on examples with explanations.

**Design of the task.**

- Blind raters to which system produced each output, and randomise order and side.
- Side-by-side comparison for sensitive detection of differences; absolute ratings for
  tracking a level over time.
- Small scales (binary or three to five points) per criterion.
- Ask for a brief justification on a subset; it improves care and helps audits.

**Sampling.** A stratified random sample of real inputs, not hand-picked ones; size from
the confidence interval you need; the same items for all systems so comparisons are paired.

**Quality control.**

- Double-label an overlap of 10-20% and report inter-rater agreement (Cohen's or Fleiss'
  kappa, Krippendorff's alpha).
- Seed gold items with known answers to estimate each rater's accuracy.
- Monitor per-rater distributions and speed; re-insert earlier items over time to detect
  drift.
- Resolve disagreements by adjudication and feed the ruling back into the guidelines.

**Interpreting low agreement.** It usually means the task is underspecified, so fix the
rubric before adding raters. Where the criterion is inherently subjective, collect several
ratings per item and report the distribution.

**Economics.** Use human labels where they have the most leverage: calibrating automated
graders, auditing samples and settling close decisions.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Agreement is high but you suspect raters are all wrong in the same way. How do you check?
- How many items and raters do you need to detect a 5-point preference difference?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="eval-032" data-area="eval" data-skill="human-eval" data-also="statistics python" data-type="coding" data-level="core" data-tracks="mle ai re"}

::: {.rv-q}
Define Cohen's kappa, compute it for a small example, and implement it. When is it misleading?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
Kappa is agreement between two raters corrected for the agreement expected by chance:

$$
\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}, \qquad p_e = \sum_k p_{1k}\,p_{2k},
$$

where $p_o$ is the observed agreement and $p_{1k}, p_{2k}$ are the fractions of items each
rater assigns to category $k$.

**Example.** 100 items; both say yes on 45, both say no on 35, and they split 10 and 10 on
the rest. $p_o = 0.80$. Each rater says yes 55% of the time, so
$p_e = 0.55^2 + 0.45^2 = 0.505$ and $\kappa = (0.80 - 0.505)/0.495 \approx 0.60$.

```python
import numpy as np

def cohens_kappa(r1, r2):
    r1, r2 = np.asarray(r1), np.asarray(r2)
    assert r1.shape == r2.shape and r1.size > 0
    labels = np.unique(np.concatenate([r1, r2]))
    index = {lab: i for i, lab in enumerate(labels)}
    C = np.zeros((len(labels), len(labels)))
    for a, b in zip(r1, r2):
        C[index[a], index[b]] += 1                 # confusion matrix between raters
    n = C.sum()
    p_o = np.trace(C) / n
    p_e = float(C.sum(axis=1) @ C.sum(axis=0)) / n**2
    return 1.0 if np.isclose(p_e, 1.0) else (p_o - p_e) / (1.0 - p_e)
```

**When it misleads.**

- *Prevalence.* If both raters say "pass" 97.5% of the time, chance agreement is already
  about 95%, so 95% observed agreement gives $\kappa \approx 0$. Report raw agreement and
  the confusion matrix alongside kappa.
- *Ordinal scales.* Plain kappa treats 4 versus 5 the same as 1 versus 5; use weighted
  kappa.
- *More than two raters, or missing ratings.* Use Fleiss' kappa or Krippendorff's alpha.
- *Thresholds.* "0.6-0.8 is substantial" is a convention, not a guarantee of adequacy.
- *Agreement is not accuracy.* Two raters can agree and both be wrong.
- *Small samples.* Report a bootstrap confidence interval.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Why is kappa near zero possible with 95% raw agreement, intuitively?
- How would you compare an LLM judge to humans using kappa?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="eval-033" data-area="eval" data-skill="red-team" data-also="guardrails safety-research" data-type="design" data-level="senior" data-tracks="ai re"}

::: {.rv-q}
How would you red-team an LLM application before launch, and how do you turn the findings into something measurable?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
**Threat model first.** What is worth protecting (user data, the ability to take actions,
the brand), who attacks (curious users, abusers, a third party planting content), and
through which surfaces (user messages, uploaded files and images, retrieved documents, tool
results, memory).

**Attack categories.**

- Jailbreaks against the content policy.
- Prompt injection, direct and through content the system reads.
- Data exfiltration, including system prompt and other users' data.
- Unsafe or unauthorised tool actions.
- Privacy leaks and harmful or biased output.
- Resource abuse: inputs that cause runaway cost or loops.

**Methods.**

- *Manual expert probing*: finds novel attacks; does not scale.
- *Automated generation*: an attacker model proposes and iteratively refines attacks
  against the target, guided by a judge of success.
- *Mutation of known attacks*: encodings, other languages, role-play framing, multi-turn
  escalation, payload splitting.
- *Domain-specific cases*: built from the application's own tools and data.

**Make it measurable.** Define success per category concretely (a canary secret appears in
the output, a forbidden tool call was executed, a classifier flags the content) and report
attack success rate per category. Measure false refusals on a benign set at the same time,
since refusing everything scores perfectly on attacks.

**Process.** Triage findings by severity and exploitability; fix at the right layer
(permissions and validation before prompt wording); add each finding to a regression suite
run on every model, prompt and tool change; repeat periodically and after capability
changes.

**Limits.** A red-team result is a lower bound on vulnerability: not finding an attack
does not show that none exists. Static attack sets go stale as models and attackers adapt.

General robustness testing uses the same frame: perturb inputs (typos, paraphrase, format
changes, distribution shift) and measure how much the metric drops.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- How do you grade whether an attack succeeded without a human reading every transcript?
- Attack success rate fell after a fix, and so did helpfulness. What do you report?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="eval-034" data-area="eval" data-skill="ml-observability" data-also="production-ml data-quality" data-type="concept" data-level="core" data-tracks="mle ai"}

::: {.rv-q}
What is the difference between data drift and concept drift, how do you detect each, and what do you do about it?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
- **Covariate (data) drift**: the input distribution $P(X)$ changes; the relation
  $P(Y \mid X)$ may be intact.
- **Prior (label) shift**: the class balance $P(Y)$ changes.
- **Concept drift**: $P(Y \mid X)$ changes. The same input now has a different right
  answer (new fraud pattern, changed user intent, a policy change).

**Detection.**

- *Inputs.* Compare a recent window with a reference per feature: population stability
  index, $\mathrm{PSI} = \sum_i (a_i - e_i)\ln(a_i/e_i)$ over bins with reference share
  $e_i$ and current share $a_i$; Kolmogorov-Smirnov or chi-square tests; for text and
  images, distances between embedding distributions or a classifier trained to tell the
  windows apart.
- *Outputs.* Shifts in the score distribution and predicted class mix.
- *Performance.* The only direct evidence of concept drift is labelled outcomes. When
  labels are delayed, use early proxies, a small fast-labelled sample, or delayed
  evaluation by cohort.

**Caveats.**

- At large volume every statistical test is significant. Alert on effect sizes with
  thresholds learned from normal week-to-week variation. Common PSI cut-offs (0.1, 0.25)
  are conventions.
- Drift is not degradation. Many input shifts do not hurt; concept drift can hurt with no
  visible input shift.
- Most drift alerts are pipeline faults: a schema change, a unit change, a spike in nulls,
  a broken upstream job. Check data quality first.

**Response.** Fix the pipeline if it is a bug. Otherwise retrain or fine-tune on recent
data, recalibrate if only the base rate moved, add features for the new pattern, or fall
back to a safer policy. Scheduled retraining with monitored evaluation handles gradual
drift; alerts handle abrupt changes.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Labels arrive 30 days late. How do you know today that the model is failing?
- Which drift alerts would you page on, and which only log?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="eval-035" data-area="eval" data-skill="ml-observability" data-also="llm-evals llm-cost" data-type="concept" data-level="senior" data-tracks="ai mle"}

::: {.rv-q}
How do you monitor the quality of an LLM product in production when you have no labels?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
**Start with traces.** One trace per user request, with a span for each model call,
retrieval and tool call, recording: inputs and outputs (under a PII policy), prompt and
model versions, tokens in and out including cached, latency including time to first token,
cost, finish reason, retries and errors, and identifiers that join it to the user session
and to downstream outcomes. OpenTelemetry is the common transport; its conventions for
generative AI are still evolving.

**Quality signals without labels.**

1. *Sampled automated grading.* Run the offline graders (validated judges and code checks
   for groundedness, format validity, policy adherence) on a sample of live traces. This
   is the closest thing to a continuous quality number.
2. *Implicit user signals.* Regenerate and rephrase rates, edits to the output before use,
   acceptance of suggestions, abandonment, escalation to a human, explicit thumbs. Each is
   biased; the trend is informative.
3. *Operational proxies.* Tool error rate, validation-retry rate, refusal rate, steps per
   task, runs ended by a budget, empty retrievals.
4. *Input drift.* Clusters of intents over time; a new cluster is a use case the eval set
   does not cover.
5. *Canaries.* A fixed set of prompts replayed on a schedule detects changes in the
   upstream model or in dependencies independent of traffic mix.

**Alerting.** Rates with baselines from normal variation, segmented by route, tenant,
model version and prompt version; comparison before and after every deploy; alerts on
cost per task and latency percentiles alongside quality.

**Close the loop.** Route low-scoring and user-flagged traces to a review queue, label
them, add them to the eval set, and periodically re-validate the online judges against
those labels.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Thumbs-down rate is 0.5% of sessions. How much can you learn from it?
- What would you sample more heavily than uniform, and how do you keep the estimate unbiased?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="eval-036" data-area="eval" data-skill="ml-observability" data-also="reliability error-analysis llm-apis" data-type="debug" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle ai"}

::: {.rv-q}
A production quality metric dropped on Tuesday and your team deployed nothing. How do you investigate?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
**Is the drop real?** Check the measurement before the system: a logging or pipeline
change, a grader or judge update, a change in sampling, missing data for part of the day.

**Characterise it.** A step or a ramp? All traffic or one slice (tenant, locale, platform,
route, model version)? The shape and scope narrow the cause more than anything else.

**Things that change without your deploy.**

- *Upstream model.* A provider updated the model behind an alias, changed a default, or
  your traffic is on a fallback model because of rate limits or an outage. Canary prompts
  and the logged model id show this.
- *Dependencies.* The retrieval index failed to refresh or was rebuilt, an embedding or
  feature service changed, a tool's API changed its response format, timeouts are
  truncating context.
- *Data.* An upstream schema or unit change, a spike in nulls, a late batch job.
- *Traffic mix.* A new customer, a campaign, bot traffic, a seasonal shift in intents.
  Compare quality at fixed mix.
- *Other teams' changes.* Feature flags, experiments, configuration, shared prompts or
  libraries.
- *Infrastructure.* Region failover, capacity limits, cache expiry.

**Method.** Line up the drop time against change logs of every dependency. Diff traces
for similar inputs before and after: retrieved context, tool results, model id, token
counts, finish reasons. Replay a fixed set of requests against the current system to see
whether the change reproduces independent of traffic.

**Mitigate and learn.** Pin or roll back the dependency, or switch route, before the root
cause is fully understood if users are affected. Then add the monitor that would have
caught it at the source: a canary, a dependency version in every trace, an index
freshness check, or a data-quality gate.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- The drop affects only one tenant. What are the first three things you check?
- How do you tell a traffic mix change from a real degradation?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-001" data-area="recsys" data-skill="recsys" data-also="retrieval ranking latency" data-type="concept" data-level="core" data-tracks="mle ai"}

::: {.rv-q}
Why do large recommendation and search systems use a multi-stage funnel instead of one model that scores everything? Walk me through the stages.
:::

::: {.rv-a}
Because cost per scored item times corpus size has to fit a latency budget of roughly 100-300 ms end to end. A model good enough to produce the final order costs on the order of 0.1-1 ms per item even batched on accelerators; a corpus has $10^6$ to $10^{10}$ items. So each stage trades model capacity for coverage.

| Stage | Input → output | Model | Optimises |
|---|---|---|---|
| Retrieval | corpus → $10^3$-$10^4$ | two-tower + ANN, inverted index, item-to-item, graph walks; several sources in parallel | recall of what later stages would rank high |
| Pre-ranking | $10^4$ → a few hundred | small two-tower or light MLP, often distilled from the ranker | agreement with the ranker at low cost |
| Ranking | hundreds → tens | large multi-task network with user-item cross features and sequence features | precise per-item predictions (click, watch time, conversion) |
| Re-ranking / blending | tens → the page | value model, diversity, business rules, ads and organic mixing | page-level utility and constraints |

Points an interviewer listens for:

- Retrieval scores user and item independently so that the item side can be indexed; ranking can afford cross features because it sees few items.
- Each stage is trained on data filtered by the stages before it, which creates selection bias; early stages should be evaluated against what the final ranker wants, not only against clicks.
- Stages must be consistent. A pre-ranker that disagrees with the ranker wastes the ranker's budget; the common remedy is to distil the ranker into the earlier stages.
- Final quality is bounded by retrieval recall, so "improve the ranker" has diminishing returns once good items are no longer reaching it.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- How would you decide how many candidates each stage should pass on?
- What breaks if you train the pre-ranker only on impressions?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-002" data-area="recsys" data-skill="retrieval" data-also="representation vector-db" data-type="concept" data-level="core" data-tracks="mle ai"}

::: {.rv-q}
Explain the two-tower retrieval model. Why is it built that way, and what does the architecture cost you?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
A user (or query) tower $f(x)$ and an item tower $g(y)$ each output a $d$-dimensional vector (typically 64-512), and the score is their dot product or cosine, $s(x,y)=\langle f(x), g(y)\rangle/\tau$. Training treats each observed (user, engaged item) pair as a positive and uses other items as negatives in a softmax or contrastive loss.

Why this shape: the item tower does not depend on the user, so all item vectors are computed offline and put in an approximate nearest-neighbour index. Serving is one forward pass of the user tower plus a top-$k$ lookup, a few milliseconds for a corpus of $10^8$ or more.

What it costs:

- **No early interaction.** The score is a bilinear form, so the model cannot use cross features such as "this user's history with this creator" or term-level matching. That is why its output is a candidate set and a ranker follows.
- **One vector per user** struggles with multiple interests; multi-vector user representations (several interest embeddings, each queried separately) trade index lookups for coverage.
- **Training signal depends on negatives.** In-batch negatives are popularity-biased and mostly easy; see the logQ correction and hard-negative mining.
- **Index freshness.** New items need an embedding and an index insert before they can be retrieved; a model update requires re-embedding the corpus and keeping user and item towers on the same version.

Details worth saying: L2-normalise and learn or tune the temperature (0.02-0.1 is common with cosine), and evaluate with recall@k against held-out engagement, not AUC.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Dot product or cosine, and why does the choice interact with popularity?
- How do you roll out a new tower version without a mismatch between user and item vectors?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-003" data-area="recsys" data-skill="retrieval" data-also="representation pytorch" data-type="coding" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle re"}

::: {.rv-q}
Write the in-batch softmax loss for a two-tower retriever, and explain and implement the logQ correction. Why is it needed?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
With in-batch negatives, item $j$ appears as a negative with probability proportional to how often it is a positive, $Q(j)$. The batch softmax is a sampled softmax with proposal $Q$, and the uncorrected optimum is $s(x,y)\approx\log\frac{P(y\mid x)}{Q(y)}+c(x)$: popular items are penalised simply for being sampled often. Importance-weighting each candidate fixes it. Since

$$\sum_{j} e^{s(x,y_j)} = \mathbb{E}_{j\sim Q}\!\left[\frac{e^{s(x,y_j)}}{Q(j)}\right],$$

replace each logit by $s^c(x,y_j)=s(x,y_j)-\log Q(j)$ during training, so the batch sum estimates the full partition function. Serve with the uncorrected $s$.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def in_batch_softmax_logq(u, v, item_ids, log_q, tau=0.05):
    """u: [B, d] user/query vectors, v: [B, d] vectors of the positive items,
    item_ids: [B] ids of those items, log_q: [B] log sampling probability of each."""
    u = F.normalize(u, dim=-1)
    v = F.normalize(v, dim=-1)
    logits = u @ v.T / tau                      # [B, B], row i = user i vs all batch items
    logits = logits - log_q[None, :]            # logQ correction, per candidate column
    dup = item_ids[:, None] == item_ids[None, :]
    dup.fill_diagonal_(False)                   # same item elsewhere in the batch
    logits = logits.masked_fill(dup, float("-inf"))
    labels = torch.arange(u.size(0), device=u.device)
    return F.cross_entropy(logits, labels)
```

Pitfalls an interviewer checks:

- The correction is applied after the temperature and only in training.
- $Q$ must be the probability of appearing in a batch under the actual sampler, estimated from stream frequencies (Yi et al., 2019, estimate it online); stale or smoothed-away estimates undo the fix.
- Mask accidental hits (the user's positive appearing as another row's item), otherwise the true item is pushed down.
- In-batch negatives never include items with no positives; mix in uniformly sampled corpus items with their own $\log Q$.
- With distributed training, gather item vectors across workers to enlarge the negative set.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- What does the model learn if you leave the correction out?
- How would you estimate Q for a stream where item popularity changes hourly?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-004" data-area="recsys" data-skill="retrieval" data-also="representation" data-type="tradeoff" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle re"}

::: {.rv-q}
Your two-tower model trains on in-batch negatives and recall has plateaued. How do hard negatives help, how do you mine them, and what goes wrong?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
Random and in-batch negatives are mostly easy: after early training their logits are far below the positive's and they contribute almost no gradient. The model learns coarse topic separation but not the fine distinctions that decide the top of the list. Hard negatives are items the current model scores close to the positive but which are not relevant.

Sources, roughly in order of difficulty:

- **Impressed but not engaged** items: realistic, but biased toward what the old system showed and often not truly negative.
- **ANN-mined**: retrieve the top few hundred for each training query with the current model and sample from ranks below the very top (for example ranks 30-200), refreshing the index periodically as in ANCE.
- **Lexical negatives** for search: high BM25 score, not relevant.
- **Ranker-rejected**: retrieved candidates that the ranking model scores low.

What goes wrong:

- **False negatives.** The hardest "negatives" are often unlabelled positives. Training on them teaches the wrong geometry and recall drops. Mitigations: skip the top ranks, filter with a cross-encoder or ranker score threshold, or use the teacher's soft score instead of a 0/1 label.
- **Collapse of the easy region.** A model trained only on hard negatives forgets to separate obviously irrelevant items, because retrieval faces the whole corpus. Keep a mix; a ratio of many easy to a few hard per positive is a typical starting point.
- **Staleness.** Negatives mined with an old checkpoint stop being hard.

Measure on recall@k against the full corpus, not on the sampled-negative loss, which rises by construction when negatives get harder.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Why do hard negatives matter more for retrieval than for the ranking stage?
- How would you detect that false negatives are the problem?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-005" data-area="recsys" data-skill="retrieval" data-also="vector-db latency" data-type="tradeoff" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle ai"}

::: {.rv-q}
Compare HNSW and IVF-PQ for serving embedding retrieval over a few hundred million vectors. What decides the choice?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
Memory is the first constraint. A 256-d float32 vector is 1 KB, so $3\times10^8$ vectors are about 300 GB before any index overhead.

**HNSW** is a multi-layer proximity graph searched greedily from the top layer. It gives the best recall-latency curve in memory (recall above 0.95 at around a millisecond is routine), and supports incremental inserts. Costs: it stores full vectors plus `M` links per node, build time is high, deletes are tombstones that degrade the graph until a rebuild, and filtered search is awkward because filtering breaks graph connectivity. Knobs: `M`, `efConstruction`, `efSearch`.

**IVF-PQ** clusters vectors into `nlist` cells with k-means and searches only the `nprobe` nearest cells; product quantisation splits each vector into `m` sub-vectors and stores a one-byte code for each, so 1 KB becomes for example 32-64 bytes. Distances are computed from lookup tables. It fits in a fraction of the memory and builds fast, but recall is lower, so the usual pattern is to over-retrieve and re-score the top few hundred with exact vectors. It degrades when the data distribution drifts from the trained centroids.

Deciding factors:

- Memory budget and corpus size: compressed IVF or a disk-based graph (DiskANN style) beyond what RAM holds.
- Update rate and deletes: frequent churn favours segment-based designs with periodic merges.
- Filters (language, region, availability): low-selectivity filters need pre-filtering or per-partition indexes, otherwise post-filtering returns too few results.
- Metric: inner product is not a metric, so check the index supports MIPS or normalise.

Always report recall@k against exact search on the production query distribution, at the target p99 latency.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Recall@100 of the index is 0.9. How do you tell whether that costs anything end to end?
- How do you handle a filter that keeps only 0.1% of the corpus?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-006" data-area="recsys" data-skill="retrieval" data-also="recsys" data-type="tradeoff" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle"}

::: {.rv-q}
Production systems run many retrieval sources in parallel. Why, and how do you merge their outputs before ranking?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
One retriever has one notion of similarity and one set of blind spots. Typical sources: a personalised two-tower, item-to-item from recent engagements, followed or subscribed sources, trending and fresh content, lexical matching for search, graph walks, and an exploration source. They differ in what they recover (long-term taste, session intent, freshness, cold items), and their failures are weakly correlated.

Merging options:

- **Quotas per source** with deduplication. Simple and stable, but quotas are hand-tuned and a weak source keeps its slots.
- **Score fusion.** Raw scores are not comparable across sources. Use rank-based fusion such as reciprocal rank fusion, $\text{RRF}(d)=\sum_s \frac{1}{k+\text{rank}_s(d)}$ with $k\approx 60$, or calibrate each source's score to a common target.
- **A learned pre-ranker** that scores the union with cheap features, including which sources returned the item and at what rank. This is the usual end state, because it lets the system shift budget toward whichever source is useful for this request.

What to watch:

- **Attribution.** Log the source of every candidate through to impressions, and measure each source's unique contribution (items only it retrieved that were shown and engaged), not its raw volume.
- **Ranker bias against new sources.** The ranker was trained on candidates from existing sources and may score a new source's items poorly at first. Evaluate a new source with an online test and consider forced exposure during ramp-up.
- **Redundancy.** Adding a source that overlaps 90% with an existing one adds latency and cost without recall.
- **Latency.** Sources run in parallel with a deadline; the merge must tolerate a missing source.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- How would you decide to retire a retrieval source?
- A new embedding retriever has better offline recall but no online gain. What do you check?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-007" data-area="recsys" data-skill="recsys" data-also="classical-ml representation" data-type="concept" data-level="core" data-tracks="mle"}

::: {.rv-q}
Explain collaborative filtering with matrix factorisation for implicit feedback, and item-to-item collaborative filtering. When are these still the right tool?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
Collaborative filtering predicts a user's preference from the behaviour of similar users, using only the interaction matrix $R\in\mathbb{R}^{U\times I}$.

**Matrix factorisation** learns $p_u, q_i\in\mathbb{R}^d$ with $\hat r_{ui}=p_u^\top q_i$. For implicit feedback (clicks, plays) there are no explicit negatives, so weighted MF (Hu, Koren and Volinsky) treats every cell as a binary preference $x_{ui}$ with confidence $c_{ui}=1+\alpha r_{ui}$:

$$\min_{P,Q}\sum_{u,i} c_{ui}\,(x_{ui}-p_u^\top q_i)^2+\lambda\big(\lVert P\rVert_F^2+\lVert Q\rVert_F^2\big).$$

Alternating least squares solves for all users with items fixed, then the reverse; each step is a closed-form ridge regression, and a standard trick makes the cost scale with the number of observed interactions rather than $U\times I$. BPR instead optimises a pairwise loss on (observed, unobserved) pairs with SGD.

**Item-to-item CF** precomputes, for each item, its nearest items by co-engagement (cosine over user vectors, or a normalised co-occurrence count with a popularity discount). At serving time, the user's recent items are looked up and the neighbours merged. It reacts to a click immediately without retraining, explains itself ("because you watched X"), and is cheap.

When they are right: as retrieval sources and strong baselines, on medium-sized catalogues, and when features are scarce. A two-tower model with only ID features is essentially MF trained with a different loss. Their limits are cold start (no interactions, no vector), no use of context or content, and popularity bias in co-occurrence counts.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Why does treating all unobserved cells as zeros not ruin the model?
- How would you make item-to-item similarities robust to very popular items?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-008" data-area="recsys" data-skill="retrieval" data-also="error-analysis ranking" data-type="debug" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle"}

::: {.rv-q}
Offline recall@1000 of your retrieval stage is high, but users and raters say the final results are poor. How do you investigate?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
First question what "recall" was measured against. Recall against logged clicks only says that retrieval reproduces what the old system already showed and users clicked. It says nothing about items the old system never surfaced, and clicked is not the same as good.

Then localise the loss stage by stage:

1. **Trace the funnel for bad sessions.** For queries with poor final results, take the items a rater or an oracle (the full ranker run on a much larger set, or human-labelled ideal results) considers best. At which stage do they disappear: never retrieved, cut by the pre-ranker, ranked low, or removed by re-ranking and filters?
2. **Pre-ranker truncation.** High recall@1000 is irrelevant if only 200 survive pre-ranking. Measure recall of the ranker's top-$k$ within the pre-ranker's output.
3. **Ranker on unfamiliar candidates.** If retrieval changed recently, the ranker scores candidates outside its training distribution; its calibration on them may be poor.
4. **Precision of the candidate set.** Recall can be high while the set is full of near-duplicates or marginally relevant items that the ranker cannot tell apart with its features.
5. **Objective mismatch.** The ranker may optimise click-through while quality complaints are about relevance, satisfaction or diversity. Check rater relevance of the top results against predicted engagement.
6. **Post-ranking logic.** Diversity rules, business boosts and deduplication can reorder the page substantially.

Fixes follow the diagnosis: train early stages on the ranker's preferences (distillation), build the evaluation set from judged relevance or an oracle ranking instead of clicks, and add a per-stage recall dashboard so the loss is visible next time.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- How do you build an "oracle" target for retrieval without human labels?
- What metric would you add for the pre-ranking stage?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-009" data-area="recsys" data-skill="ranking" data-also="dl-fundamentals feature-eng" data-type="concept" data-level="core" data-tracks="mle"}

::: {.rv-q}
Walk me through the main ranking architectures: Wide & Deep, DeepFM, DCN. Why do ranking models need explicit feature crosses when an MLP is a universal approximator?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
Ranking inputs are mostly sparse categorical features (user id, item id, category, context) embedded and concatenated with dense features. The signal is largely in interactions, such as user-language × item-language or user-segment × creator. An MLP on concatenated embeddings can represent a product of two inputs only approximately and needs many units and samples to do it, so architectures add multiplicative structure explicitly.

- **Wide & Deep**: a linear model over hand-written cross-product features (memorisation of specific co-occurrences) trained jointly with an MLP over embeddings (generalisation). Works, but the crosses are manual.
- **DeepFM**: replaces the wide part with a factorisation machine, so every pair of fields interacts through the dot product of their embeddings, with no feature engineering.
- **DCN / DCN-V2**: cross layers $x_{l+1}=x_0\odot(W_l x_l+b_l)+x_l$. Each layer raises the polynomial degree of interactions with the input by one, so $L$ layers give bounded-degree crosses up to $L+1$, in parallel or stacked with an MLP. DCN-V2 uses a full (or low-rank, mixture-of-experts) matrix $W_l$.
- Later variants learn interactions with attention over field embeddings (AutoInt) or use transformer blocks over feature tokens.

Practical points:

- Most parameters are in the embedding tables (often tens to hundreds of GB), so hashing, shared tables and dimension choices matter more than the tower depth.
- Gains between these architectures are usually small compared with gains from new features, better labels, sequence features and fresher training.
- User-item cross features computed from logs (counts and rates for this user with this creator or category) are the highest-value inputs and the main source of training-serving skew.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Why is a dot product hard for an MLP to learn?
- Where would you put a new high-cardinality feature, and how do you handle its tail?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-010" data-area="recsys" data-skill="personalization" data-also="sequence-models transformers" data-type="concept" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle re"}

::: {.rv-q}
How do ranking models use a user's behaviour history? Explain DIN-style target attention and what you do when the history has thousands of events.
:::

::: {.rv-a}
The simplest user representation mean-pools the embeddings of recent items. It is one fixed vector regardless of the candidate, so a user with several interests is blurred into their average.

**Target attention (DIN)** makes the user representation depend on the candidate. For history items $e_1..e_L$ and candidate $v$, an attention unit (an MLP over $e_j$, $v$ and their interaction) gives weights $a_j=a(e_j,v)$ and the user vector is $\sum_j a_j e_j$. Behaviours related to the candidate dominate: a candidate handbag attends to past bag purchases, not to phone browsing. The original DIN does not softmax-normalise the weights, so the strength of interest is preserved. DIEN adds a recurrent layer to model how interests evolve; transformer variants apply self-attention over the sequence, with event type, time gap and position embeddings, and then attend from the candidate.

**Cost.** Target attention runs per candidate, $O(N\cdot L)$ for $N$ candidates, so it lives in the ranking stage with $L$ in the tens to low hundreds. For lifelong histories ($L$ in the thousands or more):

- **Retrieve, then attend** (SIM): first select the top few dozen behaviours relevant to the candidate, by matching category (hard search) or by embedding similarity (soft search), then run exact attention on those.
- Hash-based approximations (ETA) pick the subset with locality-sensitive hashing.
- Precompute a user embedding offline from the long history and combine it with a real-time short sequence.

Serving details matter as much as the architecture: the short-term sequence must be fresh (events from seconds ago), and training must see the sequence as it was at request time, otherwise future events leak in.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Self-attention over the history or target attention from the candidate - when does each win?
- How do you keep the sequence feature consistent between training and serving?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-011" data-area="recsys" data-skill="multi-objective" data-also="dl-fundamentals" data-type="concept" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle re"}

::: {.rv-q}
Your ranker predicts click, like, share and watch time. Compare shared-bottom, MMoE and PLE, and tell me how you detect and handle negative transfer.
:::

::: {.rv-a}
**Shared-bottom**: one shared trunk, one small tower per task. Cheap and regularising, but when tasks conflict the shared layers are pulled in different directions and some task gets worse than its single-task model (negative transfer).

**MMoE**: $K$ expert networks shared by all tasks, and a gate per task that mixes them:

$$h^t(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K} g^t_k(x)\,e_k(x),\qquad g^t(x)=\operatorname{softmax}(W^t x).$$

Tasks can use different mixtures, so loosely related tasks interfere less. In practice gates can collapse onto the same experts.

**PLE**: separates experts into shared and task-specific groups, with gates that combine a task's own experts with the shared ones, stacked over several levels. It was proposed to address the "seesaw" pattern, where improving one task degrades another, which MMoE still shows.

Detecting negative transfer: compare each head against a single-task baseline with the same data and capacity, per task and per slice; watch for one task's loss improving while another's rises after a change in loss weights.

Handling it:

- **Loss balancing.** Tasks differ in label density and loss scale (a sparse share label versus a dense click label, a regression versus a classification). Options are manual weights, uncertainty weighting, or gradient-norm balancing; gradient-surgery methods project out conflicting gradient components.
- **Structure.** Give sparse tasks their own experts; model sequential dependence explicitly (click then convert) as ESMM does.
- **Stop-gradient** from auxiliary heads into shared embeddings when an auxiliary task hurts the main one.

Sparse tasks usually benefit most from sharing; dense tasks have the least to gain and the most to lose.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- How do you choose loss weights when one head is a regression on watch time?
- What would you look at to see whether the gates learned anything?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-012" data-area="recsys" data-skill="multi-objective" data-also="ab-testing metrics" data-type="tradeoff" data-level="staff" data-tracks="mle"}

::: {.rv-q}
The ranker outputs a dozen predictions. How do you combine them into one ranking score, and how are the weights chosen?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
The usual form is a value model, a weighted combination of calibrated predictions:

$$\text{score}=\sum_k w_k\,\hat p_k\quad\text{or}\quad \prod_k \hat p_k^{\,\alpha_k},$$

for example $w_\text{click}\,p_\text{click}+w_\text{like}\,p_\text{like}+w_\text{share}\,p_\text{share}+w_\text{time}\,\mathbb{E}[\text{watch time}]-w_\text{neg}\,p_\text{hide or report}$. The additive form reads as expected value in a common currency; the multiplicative form requires an item to be acceptable on every factor.

How weights are set:

1. **State the north-star metric** the weights serve (long-term retention, sessions per user, satisfied sessions) and guardrails (reports, creator-side health, revenue).
2. **Online tuning.** Run weight variants as A/B arms and choose by the north star. Grid search does not scale past a few weights, so teams use Bayesian optimisation or evolutionary search over online arms, sometimes with offline replay to prune the space first.
3. **Anchor to long-term outcomes.** Fit how each short-term action predicts a long-term outcome (for example survey satisfaction or retention), ideally validated by long holdouts, and use that as a starting point.

Failure modes to name:

- **Calibration drift changes the weights implicitly.** If a head is retrained and its scale shifts, the effective trade-off moves without anyone changing a weight. Keep heads calibrated and monitor the distribution of each term.
- **Short-term proxy.** Weights tuned on a two-week test favour actions with immediate payoff, such as clickbait; long-running holdouts are the check.
- **Constraint handling.** Some goals are constraints, not terms (minimum exposure for new creators, a cap on negative feedback). A Lagrangian formulation gives each a multiplier that is adjusted to meet its target.
- **Organisational coupling.** Every team wants its prediction in the formula; a shared process for evaluating new terms matters as much as the optimiser.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Why must the heads be calibrated for the weights to be meaningful?
- How would you personalise the weights, and what is the risk?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-013" data-area="recsys" data-skill="ranking" data-also="training-dynamics" data-type="concept" data-level="core" data-tracks="mle re"}

::: {.rv-q}
Compare pointwise, pairwise and listwise learning to rank. Which would you use for a feed ranker and which for web-search relevance?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
They differ in what a training example is and therefore in what the loss can see.

- **Pointwise**: each (query, item) is an independent example with a classification or regression loss, for example binary cross-entropy on click. The output is an absolute prediction, which can be calibrated and combined with other predictions. It ignores that only relative order within a list matters and spends capacity on separating queries from each other.
- **Pairwise**: examples are pairs from the same query, with a loss on the score difference, such as RankNet $\log(1+e^{-(s_i-s_j)})$ for $i$ preferred to $j$, BPR, or hinge. It optimises order directly and cancels per-query offsets (some bias terms drop out), but treats all pairs alike, so an error at rank 50 costs as much as one at rank 1, and scores are not probabilities.
- **Listwise**: the loss is defined on the whole list: softmax cross-entropy over the list (ListNet top-one), or metric-driven methods such as LambdaRank/LambdaMART and approximate-NDCG. Matches top-heavy metrics best; needs the lists to be grouped and is sensitive to list length and label noise.

Choice:

- **Feed and ads ranking**: pointwise multi-task heads, because the system needs calibrated probabilities for a value model or an auction, and labels are per-impression engagement events. Pairwise or listwise terms are sometimes added as auxiliary losses to improve order.
- **Search relevance with graded judgments**: listwise or LambdaMART-style objectives on NDCG, because labels are graded per query and only the order within a query matters.
- **Retrieval**: sampled softmax, which is listwise over the positive and sampled negatives.

A common hybrid trains a calibrated pointwise loss plus a pairwise or listwise loss, to get both a usable probability and a better order.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Why are pairwise scores not calibrated, and can you fix that after the fact?
- What does the per-query grouping do to how you split train and test data?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-014" data-area="recsys" data-skill="ranking" data-also="classical-ml" data-type="derivation" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle re"}

::: {.rv-q}
NDCG is not differentiable. Explain how LambdaRank gets around that and what LambdaMART adds.
:::

::: {.rv-a}
NDCG depends on scores only through the sort order, so it is piecewise constant in the scores: the gradient is zero almost everywhere and undefined at ties.

**RankNet** starts from a pairwise logistic loss. For documents $i,j$ in the same query with $i$ more relevant, $C_{ij}=\log\big(1+e^{-\sigma(s_i-s_j)}\big)$, and

$$\lambda_{ij}\equiv\frac{\partial C_{ij}}{\partial s_i}=-\frac{\sigma}{1+e^{\sigma(s_i-s_j)}}=-\frac{\partial C_{ij}}{\partial s_j}.$$

**LambdaRank** observes that training only needs gradients, not a loss. It scales each pair's gradient by how much the metric would change if the two documents swapped positions in the current ranking:

$$\lambda_{ij}=-\frac{\sigma}{1+e^{\sigma(s_i-s_j)}}\;\big|\Delta\text{NDCG}_{ij}\big|,\qquad \lambda_i=\sum_{j:(i,j)}\lambda_{ij}-\sum_{j:(j,i)}\lambda_{ji}.$$

Each document receives a net force: up if it is more relevant than documents it is confused with, down otherwise, with pairs near the top of the list weighted more because swapping them changes NDCG more. Empirically this optimises NDCG well, and later work showed the lambdas correspond to the gradient of a bound on the metric.

**LambdaMART** plugs these lambdas into gradient-boosted regression trees: each tree is fit to the per-document lambdas, and leaf values use a Newton step with the second derivatives. It is the `lambdarank` objective in LightGBM and `rank:ndcg` in XGBoost.

Why it is still a strong baseline: it handles heterogeneous, unnormalised dense features (BM25 scores, counts, quality signals) with little tuning and trains on modest amounts of judged data. Its limits are sparse high-cardinality ids and raw text, which need embeddings, and incremental training.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Why weight by the NDCG change of a swap rather than by the positions directly?
- What happens to the lambdas for a query whose documents all have the same label?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-015" data-area="recsys" data-skill="ranking" data-also="metrics python" data-type="coding" data-level="core" data-tracks="mle ai re"}

::: {.rv-q}
Implement NDCG@k for one query, then tell me the choices and edge cases that change the number.
:::

::: {.rv-a}
$$\text{DCG@}k=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{2^{rel_i}-1}{\log_2(i+1)},\qquad \text{NDCG@}k=\frac{\text{DCG@}k}{\text{IDCG@}k},$$

where $rel_i$ is the graded label of the item at rank $i$ and IDCG is the DCG of the ideal ordering.

```python
import numpy as np

def dcg_at_k(rels, k, exp_gain=True):
    rels = np.asarray(rels, dtype=float)[:k]
    gains = 2.0 ** rels - 1.0 if exp_gain else rels
    discounts = 1.0 / np.log2(np.arange(2, rels.size + 2))   # ranks 1..k -> log2(2..k+1)
    return float((gains * discounts).sum())

def ndcg_at_k(scores, labels, k, exp_gain=True):
    scores, labels = np.asarray(scores), np.asarray(labels)
    order = np.argsort(-scores, kind="stable")
    ideal = dcg_at_k(np.sort(labels)[::-1], k, exp_gain)     # ideal over ALL labelled items
    if ideal == 0.0:
        return None                                          # no relevant item: undefined
    return dcg_at_k(labels[order], k, exp_gain) / ideal

def mean_ndcg(queries, k):
    vals = [ndcg_at_k(s, l, k) for s, l in queries]
    vals = [v for v in vals if v is not None]
    return float(np.mean(vals)) if vals else float("nan")
```

What an interviewer checks:

- **Ideal ranking** is computed from all judged items for the query, not from the top $k$ of the model's ranking; the latter inflates the score.
- **Queries with no relevant item**: skip them or count them as 0 or 1. Each convention gives a different mean, so state which one you use and keep it fixed across systems.
- **Gain function**: exponential gain $2^{rel}-1$ emphasises the top grade; linear gain is also common. The two are identical for binary labels.
- **Ties in scores** make the result depend on sort order; use a stable sort and a fixed tie-break, or average over tie permutations.
- **Unjudged items** are usually treated as non-relevant, which penalises systems that retrieve new items the judging pool never saw.
- **Average per query**, not over pooled documents, and report confidence intervals over queries.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- How does NDCG differ from MRR and MAP in what it rewards?
- Your new retriever surfaces many unjudged documents and NDCG drops. What do you do?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-016" data-area="recsys" data-skill="ranking" data-also="causal" data-type="concept" data-level="core" data-tracks="mle re"}

::: {.rv-q}
What is position bias in click data, and what are the standard ways to keep it out of a ranking model?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
Users click more on higher positions regardless of relevance, so a model trained on raw clicks learns "was shown at the top" as evidence of quality and reinforces the existing order. The usual formalisation is the examination hypothesis:

$$P(\text{click}\mid q,d,k)=\underbrace{P(\text{examined}\mid k)}_{\theta_k}\cdot P(\text{relevant}\mid q,d).$$

Three standard treatments:

- **Position as a feature.** Feed the position (and device, surface) during training and set it to a fixed value at serving, so the model attributes the positional effect to that input. A variant uses a separate shallow "bias tower" whose logit is added to the main logit in training and dropped at serving, with dropout on the position input so the main tower does not ignore relevance. It is simple and widely used, but the separation is only as good as the additive (or multiplicative) assumption.
- **Inverse propensity weighting.** Weight each clicked example by $1/\theta_k$. Under the examination model this gives an unbiased estimate of the relevance-based loss. Variance grows for low positions, so propensities are clipped.
- **Randomisation.** Estimate $\theta_k$, or collect unbiased data directly, by randomising order on a small slice of traffic: full shuffles of the top $n$ are costly to users, so pair swaps of adjacent positions are preferred. Propensities can also be estimated without intervention by jointly fitting examination and relevance (EM-style or dual-learning methods), or by harvesting cases where different rankers placed the same item at different positions.

Position bias is one of several biases in the same logs: selection bias (only shown items have labels), trust bias (users click top results even when they look irrelevant), and context effects from neighbouring items.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- What value do you set the position feature to at serving time, and does it matter?
- Why does IPS fail when the logging policy is deterministic?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-017" data-area="recsys" data-skill="ranking" data-also="ab-testing causal evals" data-type="tradeoff" data-level="staff" data-tracks="mle re"}

::: {.rv-q}
You want to evaluate a new ranking policy before a full A/B test. Compare offline replay, counterfactual estimators and interleaving. What does each one assume?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
**Standard offline metrics** (AUC, NDCG on logged impressions) evaluate the new model only on items the old policy chose to show. They cannot credit it for surfacing items that were never shown.

**Offline replay.** If a slice of traffic was served uniformly at random, replay the log and keep only events where the new policy would have chosen the logged action; the average reward on those is an unbiased estimate of the new policy's value. It needs random logging and discards most data when the action space is large.

**Counterfactual (off-policy) estimators** reweight logs from a stochastic logging policy $\pi_0$:

$$\hat V_\text{IPS}=\frac1n\sum_i\frac{\pi(a_i\mid x_i)}{\pi_0(a_i\mid x_i)}\,r_i.$$

Unbiased if $\pi_0$ has support wherever $\pi$ does and propensities are logged correctly. Variance explodes when the policies differ, so practice uses clipping, self-normalisation (SNIPS: divide by the sum of weights) and doubly robust estimators, which add a reward model and stay consistent if either the model or the propensities are right. For slates the action space is combinatorial, so estimators assume structure, such as reward that decomposes over positions.

**Interleaving.** Merge the two rankers' lists for the same request (team-draft: the rankers alternately pick their best remaining item) and credit clicks to the ranker that contributed the item. Each user is their own control, so it is reported to need one to two orders of magnitude less traffic than an A/B test to detect a preference. It measures relative click preference between two rankers for the same list position, not absolute metrics, retention or revenue, and does not apply cleanly to whole-page or multi-objective changes.

A sensible sequence: offline metrics to reject bad candidates, counterfactual estimates or interleaving to rank the survivors, then an A/B test for the decision metrics and guardrails.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- How would you check that your logged propensities are correct?
- Interleaving says B wins but the A/B test is flat. What could explain it?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-018" data-area="recsys" data-skill="ads" data-also="bayesian classical-ml" data-type="concept" data-level="core" data-tracks="mle"}

::: {.rv-q}
You train a CTR model on data where negatives were downsampled to 10%. What does the model output, how do you correct it, and how do you check calibration afterwards?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
It outputs the click probability in the sampled population, which is too high. If positives are all kept and negatives kept with probability $s$, Bayes' rule gives the true probability from the sampled one $p_s$:

$$p=\frac{s\,p_s}{1-p_s+s\,p_s},\qquad \operatorname{logit}(p)=\operatorname{logit}(p_s)+\log s.$$

So the correction is a constant shift of the logit by $\log s$; equivalently, add $\log s$ to the bias at serving, or train with negatives weighted by $1/s$. With $s=0.1$ and $p_s=0.2$ the corrected value is about $0.0244$, not $0.02$: multiplying by $s$ is only the small-probability approximation. Apply exactly one correction; weighting the loss and also shifting the logit double-corrects.

Downsampling is used because clicks are rare (often well under 5%) and most negatives are redundant; it cuts training cost with little loss of ranking quality. It does not change the order of scores, only their scale.

Checking calibration:

- **Aggregate bias**: sum of predictions over sum of observed clicks, on a later time window with the production (unsampled) distribution. Target is close to 1.
- **Reliability by score bucket** and **by slice** (placement, country, advertiser, new versus old items). A model can be right on average and wrong in opposite directions across slices.
- **Log loss or normalised cross-entropy** relative to predicting the base rate, alongside AUC. AUC is blind to calibration.

If residual miscalibration remains, fit a post-hoc calibrator (Platt scaling or isotonic regression) on recent held-out data, and refit it whenever the model or the traffic mix changes.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- What changes if the sampling rate depends on features, for example by placement?
- Why does AUC not move when you apply the correction?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-019" data-area="recsys" data-skill="ads" data-also="production-ml" data-type="tradeoff" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle"}

::: {.rv-q}
Conversions can arrive days after the click. How do you train a CVR model that is both fresh and correctly labelled?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
The conflict: a click without a conversion so far is not a negative, it is censored. Training on recent data labels slow converters as negatives and biases predicted CVR downward, most strongly for new campaigns; waiting for the full attribution window (for example 7 days after the click) gives correct labels but a model that is a week stale, which hurts on new ads and shifting traffic.

Options:

1. **Wait for maturity.** Train only on clicks older than the window. Correct, simple, stale. Reasonable when most conversions arrive quickly and campaigns are long-lived.
2. **Short window plus correction.** Use a waiting window that captures most conversions (say the first hour or day) and correct for the rest with an estimate of the fraction that arrives later, per advertiser or conversion type.
3. **Model the delay.** The delayed feedback model (Chapelle, 2014) jointly fits the conversion probability and a delay distribution, so an unconverted click of age $t$ contributes the likelihood of "either will not convert, or will convert after $t$".
4. **Label correction in streaming training.** Ingest every click immediately as a negative and insert a positive when the conversion arrives, with importance weights that make the loss unbiased in expectation (the fake-negative weighted family of methods).
5. **Auxiliary fast signals.** Add heads for early events (add-to-cart, page dwell) that arrive quickly and correlate with conversion.

What to check: calibration by click age and by campaign age, since delay bias shows up as under-prediction on recent traffic; the calibration layer must also be fitted on matured labels. Attribution rules (last click, view-through, window length) define the label, so a change in them is a label shift.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- How would you measure the conversion delay distribution without bias from censoring?
- What happens to auto-bidding campaigns if CVR is under-predicted for new ads?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-020" data-area="recsys" data-skill="ads" data-also="multi-objective causal" data-type="concept" data-level="senior" data-tracks="mle re"}

::: {.rv-q}
What problem does ESMM solve in conversion-rate modelling, and how? Is its CVR estimate unbiased?
:::

::: {.rv-a}
A conventional CVR model is trained on clicked impressions, because conversion labels only exist after a click, but at serving it scores all candidate impressions. That is **sample selection bias**: the clicked population is not a random sample of impressions. It also suffers **data sparsity**, since clicks are a few percent of impressions and conversions a few percent of clicks.

ESMM (entire-space multi-task model) uses the identity

$$\underbrace{P(\text{click},\text{conv}\mid x)}_{\text{pCTCVR}}=\underbrace{P(\text{click}\mid x)}_{\text{pCTR}}\cdot\underbrace{P(\text{conv}\mid \text{click},x)}_{\text{pCVR}}.$$

Two towers over shared embeddings output pCTR and pCVR. The losses are binary cross-entropy on click and on click-and-convert, both defined on **all impressions**. There is no loss on pCVR directly; it is learned as the factor that makes the product fit. The CVR tower therefore trains on the same input space it serves on, and the embeddings are learned from abundant click data.

Caveats a senior answer includes:

- It is not guaranteed unbiased. pCVR is identified only through the product, so errors in pCTR are absorbed by pCVR, and where pCTR is tiny the CVR tower gets almost no gradient. Later work (the ESCM² line) argues the estimate remains biased and adds inverse-propensity or doubly robust terms on the click space.
- The product of two individually reasonable scores need not be calibrated; check pCTCVR on impressions and pCVR on clicks separately.
- It models conversion given the logged serving policy, not a causal effect of showing the ad.
- The same idea extends to longer funnels (click, add-to-cart, purchase), and delayed conversions still need separate treatment.
:::

::: {.rv-probes}
- Why not just train the CVR tower on clicked samples with inverse-propensity weights?
- Which metric would reveal that pCVR is absorbing pCTR errors?
:::

::::

:::: {.rv-card data-id="recsys-021" data-area="recsys" data-skill="ads" data-also="" data-type="concept" data-level="core" data-tracks="mle"}

::: {.rv-q}
How does an ads auction rank and price ads? Give me eCPM for different bid types, the generalised second-price payment, and how VCG differs.
:::

::: {.rv-a}
**Ranking.** Advertisers bid on different events, so bids are converted to expected value per thousand impressions:

- CPM bid: $\text{eCPM}=\text{bid}$.
- CPC bid: $\text{eCPM}=1000\cdot\text{bid}_\text{click}\cdot p\text{CTR}$.
- CPA / optimised bidding: $\text{eCPM}=1000\cdot\text{bid}_\text{conv}\cdot p\text{CTR}\cdot p\text{CVR}$.

Many platforms rank by a total value that adds a quality or user-experience term, so a relevant ad can beat a higher bid.

**Generalised second price (GSP).** Each winner pays the minimum needed to keep its slot. For CPC ads ranked by $\text{bid}\times p\text{CTR}$:
